meta.title: Tideline Fishing Coach knowledge base - Chesapeake Bay & Mid-Atlantic offshore
meta.regsPolicy: Every regulation here is a snapshot for orientation only and is marked 'check current regs'. Seasons, slots and creel limits change yearly (sometimes mid-season). The coach must always point to the official link and never state a limit as definitive.
meta.waterTempNote: waterTempF ranges are approximate comfort/activity ranges from angler literature and reports, not hard limits; offshore ranges come from inthespread.com SST guide.

species.name: Striped bass (rockfish)
species.season: Year-round presence in the Bay; spring catch-and-release, summer shallow topwater bite early/late, fall is prime as water drops through the 60s (Oct 2026 main Bay upper 60s F).
species.where: Channel edges (e.g., Buoy 83 to Sharps Island Light, fish suspended ~30 ft), Bay Bridge piers and the 30-ft east-side edge, lumps (Pooles Island, Love Point), rocky shorelines, docks and points, creek mouths, OC Inlet/Route 50 Bridge pilings and jetties.
species.tide: Moving water; fish position on the down-current side of structure; early morning and evening low-light windows matter most in summer.
methods: Trolling umbrella rigs and tandems with Tsunami shads at ~2.5-3.0 kn (sometimes under 2 kn); turn to vary bait depth (Capt. Billy Gee).
Live-lining spot (summer) or eels (fall, Pooles Island/Love Point) on channel edges and lumps.
Casting topwater, paddletails, jerkbaits to shorelines and pilings at dawn/dusk; vertical soft-plastic jigging under birds and on suspended marks.
species.regsNote: check current regs - MD 2026 Chesapeake: C&R Jan 1-Apr 30; harvest May 1-Jul 31 and Sep 1-Dec 5; CLOSED Aug 1-31; C&R Dec 6-31; 1 fish/person/day 19-24 in. Spawning rivers closed to targeting Mar 1-May 31; through May 15 no stingers, max 6 trolling rods, barbless hooks when trolling. Ocean: 1 fish 28-31 in. Potomac main stem = PRFC rules. Virginia differs (VMRC).
species.say: Rockfish are on the channel edges and bridge piers right now; work the moving tide early or late, and remember Maryland's 19-24 inch, one-fish slot - check DNR before you keep one.

species.name: Bluefish
species.season: Late spring through fall in the Bay; fall run in lower Bay channels and OC surf/inlet.
species.where: Lower Bay shipping channel edges (east side below Hoopers Island), Potomac mouth, Tangier Sound, middle Bay Buoy 83-Sharps Island edge; OC inlet, Route 50 Bridge, surf; 30 Fathom Lumps offshore.
species.tide: Outgoing tide at the OC inlet for drifting cut bait; moving water generally.
methods: Trolling surgical tubes behind planers or inline weights; umbrella rigs with spoons for larger fall fish.
Drifting cut bait or casting soft-plastic jigs on the inlet ebb.
Casting metal or popping plugs into breaking fish; use a short wire or heavy leader.
species.regsNote: check current regs - MD (secondary source, 2024): 8 in min; 3/person private, 5 for-hire. Verify with DNR/VMRC.
species.say: If you see blues slashing, troll tubes or spoons along the channel edge with some weight to get down, and bring a leader - they'll bite through light line.

species.name: Spanish mackerel
species.season: Mid-summer into early fall (roughly July-September) in middle and lower Bay; abundance varies year to year.
species.where: Lower Bay channel edges, Potomac mouth, Tangier Sound, middle Bay Buoy 83-Sharps Island edge; reef structure; under birds and near slicks.
species.tide: Moving water along edges; follow bait and birds rather than a fixed tide window.
methods: Fast trolling small Drone/Clark spoons (size 0-1) behind #1-#3 planers at ~6 kn (some go faster); slow toward ~3.5 kn on hookup.
15-20 lb fluorocarbon leaders; ball-bearing swivels to stop twist.
Casting small metal fast with rod tip low, letting it sink 15-20 ft; work the outside edge of a busting school.
species.regsNote: check current regs - MD (secondary 2024): 14 in min. Verify DNR/VMRC.
species.say: Mackerel like speed - troll small spoons on planers around 6 knots to find them, then slow down once you hook up.

species.name: Cobia
species.season: Roughly Memorial Day through September in the lower Bay (Virginia core); MD season is short (2026: Jun 15-Sep 20).
species.where: Lower Bay: drop-offs in 15-25 ft (e.g., red 72, Rappahannock Spit, Latimer Shoals); around buoys, pilings, bridges, bait pods, rays.
species.tide: Current matters mostly for chum slick and boat position; set slick along the shelf.
methods: Sight casting from a tower on calm, sunny days: live eels, artificial eels, bucktails, or chuggers cast just ahead of cruising fish.
Anchored chumming on a drop-off with ground bunker; live eels and bunker chunks on 10/0 circle hooks, 50 lb fluoro leader.
Have a second rod ready - a follower often trails a hooked cobia.
species.regsNote: check current regs - MD 2026: Jun 15-Sep 20; 43 in TL min; 1/angler/day; max 2/boat if 2+ aboard. Virginia has its own season/vessel limits (VMRC).
species.say: Calm, bright day in the lower Bay? Get up high and look for cobia around buoys and rays - have a live eel ready to cast ahead of them, and check the season dates first.

species.name: Red drum (redfish/puppy drum)
species.season: Summer-fall in the lower Bay (slot fish); big bull reds in the OC/VA/OBX surf in fall.
species.where: Lower Potomac, lower Patuxent, Hoopers Island, Tangier Sound shorelines and creek mouths; shoals, ledges, reefs and wrecks in 15-30 ft; ocean surf.
species.tide: Tide switch reported best by guides; drift soft crab on outgoing tide from tidal creeks.
methods: Topwater and paddletails along shorelines and grass edges.
Fresh cut bait (spot, croaker, menhaden) or peeler crab on fish-finder rigs with 8/0 circle hooks on shoals.
Surf: cut mullet or menhaden for big reds; release oversized fish quickly.
species.regsNote: check current regs - MD (secondary 2024): 18-27 in slot, 1/day. VA/NC differ.
species.say: Reds are feeding around the lower Bay shoals - try fresh cut spot on a fish-finder rig around the tide change, and only keep one in the slot if your state allows.

species.name: Speckled trout (spotted seatrout)
species.season: Late summer through fall, bite improves as water cools; lower Bay and Tangier/Pocomoke.
species.where: Shallow eelgrass beds in 2-6 ft (flats near Smith and Tangier islands), marsh points, Patuxent mouth, Point Lookout.
species.tide: Moving water over grass; dawn topwater window.
methods: Popping cork with paddletail or shrimp-imitation soft plastic over grass.
Early-morning topwater on the flats.
Live-lining spot for larger fish.
species.regsNote: check current regs - MD (secondary 2024): 14 in min. Verify DNR/VMRC.
species.say: Specks love shallow grass in two to six feet - pop a cork with a paddletail over the flats early, and the bite gets better as the water cools.

species.name: White perch
species.season: Year-round; shallow structure in summer, moving to deeper lower-river water as temperatures drop in late fall.
species.where: Tidal-river shoreline structure, docks, piers, oyster bars, Kent Narrows, west side of the Bay Bridge in ~15 ft.
species.tide: Structure plus current is key; early morning and evening.
methods: Small spinnerbaits, spinners, spin-jigs cast to cover at low light.
Bottom rig with grass shrimp, peeler crab or bloodworm on oyster bars and pier pilings.
Great kid/family target - light tackle.
species.regsNote: check current regs - generally no closed season in MD tidal water; verify DNR.
species.say: For a fun, easy bite, toss a small spinnerbait to docks and oyster bars in the rivers early or late, or drop grass shrimp on a bottom rig.

species.name: Summer flounder (fluke)
species.season: Late spring to fall; fall fish exit the OC back bays through the inlet channels to the ocean.
species.where: OC East Channel, West Channel and inlet channels; inshore lumps outside the inlet; nearshore wrecks; lower Bay near Point Lookout, Tangier and Pocomoke sounds.
species.tide: Flood tide best at OC inlet (clearer water, especially East Channel).
methods: Drifting squid/minnow rigs for numbers; live spot or peanut bunker for bigger fish.
Bucktail or jighead with white/pink Gulp! on the drift.
Watch channel boat traffic while drifting.
species.regsNote: check current regs - MD 2026: open all year; 4/day; 16 in Jan 1-May 31, 17.5 in Jun 1-Dec 31.
species.say: Fish the incoming tide in the East Channel where the water's clearest, drift a Gulp or live spot, and remember the 17.5-inch minimum this summer and fall - verify with DNR.

species.name: Black sea bass
species.season: Spring through December on ocean wrecks and reefs; cold months strong; seasons have in-year closures.
species.where: Nearshore and offshore wrecks, artificial reefs, rock piles (e.g., 30-ft rock pile off OC).
species.tide: Anchor or drift over structure; easier on slower current.
methods: Hi-lo bottom rigs with squid, clams, crab or shrimp.
Jigging spoons or bucktails over the structure.
Anchor precisely up-current of the wreck.
species.regsNote: check current regs - MD (secondary 2024): 13 in, 15/person; split season with fall reopening. Federal/state seasons shift yearly.
species.say: Sea bass are stacking on the wrecks and reefs - anchor up-current and drop a hi-lo rig with squid or clam, but check the season's open dates first.

species.name: Tautog (togs/blackfish)
species.season: Fall and spring as water cools; jetty rocks first in late October, then nearshore wrecks.
species.where: OC inlet jetties, Route 50 Bridge, nearshore wrecks and rock piles, mussel beds, usually under 60 ft.
species.tide: Many anglers favor slower water around slack (practice, not well documented); dawn/dusk feeding peaks.
methods: Green crab or sand fleas on a short-dropper bottom rig, 4/0 hook, heavy leader.
Tog jigs with crab on rock piles.
30-40 lb braid to feel the crunch; set firmly - togs crush and spit baits.
species.regsNote: check current regs - MD (secondary 2024): 16 in; creel varies by season incl. a C&R-only window in late spring. Verify DNR/VMRC.
species.say: Togs are on the inlet rocks now - fish a piece of green crab tight to the structure and be ready to lose a few rigs.

species.name: Dolphin (mahi-mahi)
species.season: Roughly late April/June through September-October offshore; best in warm water, slows as it cools.
species.where: Weedlines, floating debris, lobster-pot buoys/high fliers, temperature breaks inside and outside the canyons.
species.tide: Offshore - follow current edges and convergence lines rather than tide.
methods: Troll small ballyhoo and skirted baits ~4 kn along weedlines; be first to the grass.
Once a school is found, keep one fish hooked and bail with cut squid/strip baits.
Pot-hop: check each high flier with a short pass or a pitch bait.
species.regsNote: check current regs - MD page lists 10/person, 54/boat (secondary); federal (SAFMC/NOAA) rules apply in federal waters.
species.say: Look for a weedline or pot buoy on the warm side of the break, troll slow past it, and keep that first mahi in the water so the school stays with the boat.

species.name: Yellowfin tuna
species.season: Summer into fall in the canyons (good early-October reports in recent years).
species.where: Baltimore, Poorman's, Washington, Norfolk canyons; canyon walls, the bight, canyon tips; warm side of temperature breaks.
species.tide: Offshore - current edges, rips, eddies at the canyon heads.
methods: Troll ballyhoo, skirted lures, spreader bars and daisy chains at ~5-7 kn (lures up to 7-10 kn).
Work up and down the walls where currents upwell nutrients; watch for pilot whales and common dolphin.
Chunking/jigging at night or over marks is common (practice; verify current local reports).
species.regsNote: check current regs - HMS Angling permit required; federal yellowfin size/bag set by NOAA HMS and adjustable in-season. Verify with HMS compliance guide.
species.say: Yellowfin like the warm edge of a break along the canyon walls - troll the wall and the tip at 6-7 knots and watch for pilot whales; make sure your HMS permit is current.

species.name: Bluefin tuna
species.season: Bursts early (late spring) and late (fall/winter) in the season; near canyon edges and shoals rather than deep canyons; also inshore winter fish off VA/OBX.
species.where: Canyon edges, offshore lumps, cooler side of breaks; nearshore in winter off Virginia/NC.
species.tide: Offshore - fronts where cool green water meets warmer current.
methods: Troll spreader bars, daisy chains and ballyhoo.
Jigging and casting to surface-feeding schools.
Heavy tackle and a plan for the fight - big fish are often out of the legal size class.
species.regsNote: check current regs - 2026: open Jun 1-Dec 31 unless modified; 27 to <73 in CFL; per vessel/day: private 2, charter 3, headboat 6, only 1 may be 47 to <73 in. Report every retained fish and dead discard within 24 h via HMS Permit Shop, HMS Catch Reporting app, or 888-872-8862. Limits are adjusted in-season.
species.say: Bluefin rules change during the season - confirm today's retention limit with NOAA and report any fish you keep within 24 hours.

species.name: White marlin
species.season: Arrive late June, peak late August, strong through September; bite ends abruptly at the first cold snap. White Marlin Open runs from Ocean City each August.
species.where: Canyon edges from Hudson to Norfolk (western edges to ~50 fathoms or shallower), warm eddies off the Gulf Stream, rip lines, temperature breaks, bait pods, birds (storm petrels).
species.tide: Offshore - eddies and rips; work bait concentrations.
methods: Troll 5.5-6.5 kn: small ballyhoo on rigger and flat lines; dredges (red/pink squid) and daisy-chain/spreader-bar teasers.
Pitch-bait and drop back when a fish shows in the spread.
Non-offset circle hooks on natural baits (required for billfish tournaments, best practice always); keep the fish in the water for release.
species.regsNote: check current regs - federal: 66 in LJFL min (white marlin/roundscale spearfish); HMS Angling or Charter/Headboat permit required; combined US landings cap of 250 blue/white marlin and roundscale spearfish per year; non-offset circle hooks with natural bait in billfish tournaments. Tournaments set higher minimums (WMO 2024: 70 lb and 70 in). Recreational billfish landings must be reported.
species.say: Look for a warm eddy or rip on the canyon edge with bait under it, troll small ballyhoo around 6 knots on circle hooks, and plan to release - keep that marlin in the water.

species.name: Wahoo
species.season: Summer through fall in the canyons; boats that put in time on structure find them.
species.where: Drop-offs, ledges, canyon walls and offshore structure, sharp temperature breaks near structure.
species.tide: Current flow affects positioning along structure - time passes with the flow.
methods: High-speed trolling 12-18 kn with weighted lures that track straight.
Wire leaders are mandatory.
Also caught incidentally in the regular tuna/marlin spread.
species.regsNote: check current regs - federal (SAFMC/NOAA) bag limits apply; verify before trip.
species.say: Wahoo want speed and wire - make a high-speed pass along the canyon wall at 12-plus knots between your tuna trolls.

conditions.say: Fish usually feed best when the water is moving - plan to be on your spot for the last of one tide and the start of the next, and use slack to reposition.
conditions.evidence: strong (consistent across DNR and guide reports)

conditions.cue: above-average tidal currents around new/full moon
conditions.say: Spring tides this week mean stronger current - use heavier jigs or sinkers and expect a tighter bite window around the turns.
conditions.evidence: moderate (DNR flags these weekly; effect on catch not quantified)

conditions.cue: temperature break offshore (e.g., 2°F or more change over a short distance)
conditions.say: That edge where the temperature jumps a couple of degrees is your structure out here - troll along it, especially where it bulges or meets the canyon wall.
conditions.evidence: strong (standard practice; 1-2°F matters, 3-5°F is a true front)

conditions.cue: temp break lines up with chlorophyll/color edge
conditions.say: When the temperature break and the green-to-blue color edge line up, that's the best-looking water on the chart.
The satellite can't see through clouds, so look at several days of composites and expect the break to have drifted with the current.
Canyon water is green and off-color right now - many boats are deep dropping for tilefish instead of trolling.
Diving birds mean bait is being pushed up - ease in on the edge, don't run through the school, and cast or troll the outside.
Birds resting on the water usually means the feed's over - keep trolling nearby and watch the sounder for fish moving along the edge.
Pilot whales and dolphin feed on squid too - tuna are often nearby, so work that area.
Wind against the current is stacking up steep, short chop - expect a rougher ride than the forecast says, and be very careful at inlets on the ebb.
Lots of anglers swear by the bite before a front, but the evidence is mostly anecdotal - the bigger concern is that the weather is changing, so watch the sky and be ready to head in.
Moon phase effects are mixed and species-specific - research shows bright moons push tuna deeper, but there's no reliable best-moon rule, so let tide and water conditions guide you.
conditions.evidence: weak/mixed (2024 review of 190 studies: catch-rate link only for swordfish; a 2007 Australian tournament study found phase effects for some species)

conditions.cue: hot water / low oxygen summer (striper stress)
conditions.say: It's hot - if you're catching and releasing rockfish, keep them in the water, use circle hooks, and consider fishing early or giving them a break.
Shallow-water topwater is best at first light, last light, or under clouds.
As the water cools through the 60s, rockfish and specks move shallow and feed hard, and perch slide to deeper river water.

speedsBySpecies.note: Sometimes under 2 kn; lines shouldn't be bar-tight or fouled with grass.
Too fast makes plugs spin; live bait barely moving.
Inferred from mixed-spread practice; inline weights to get down in fall.

speedMeasurement.say: Your GPS shows speed over the bottom; your lures care about speed through the water, so check the paddlewheel and adjust when running with or against current.

spreadBasics.say: Run the smallest spoons closest on #3 planers with short fluoro leaders for mackerel, bigger spoons on the outside #1 planers for rockfish.
In summer, 5-8 lines of 1-2 oz tandems with 4-12 oz weights is plenty; turn gently to vary depth.
Two rigger baits back behind the teasers, two flat lines close, dredges and daisy chains up front, and pitch baits ready in the cockpit.
On a multiple hookup, keep the first fish in the water and slowly circle - more fish often follow.
Through May 15, Maryland striped bass trolling is limited to six rods with barbless hooks and no stingers.

canyons.name: Baltimore Canyon
canyons.note: Day-trip range from OC; a classic marlin/tuna canyon.

canyons.name: Poorman's Canyon
canyons.note: Closest to OC inlet at ~53 nm.

canyons.name: Norfolk Canyon
canyons.note: Southernmost of the OC group, ~75 nm from OC; closer for Virginia Beach boats.

canyonTactics.say: Troll the walls where currents push nutrients up, the bight where the edge turns, and the canyon tip where eddies and rips form temperature barriers.

dolphin.say: Find a weedline, debris, or lobster-pot high flier on warm water, troll slow past it, then keep one fish hooked and bail with cut bait.

deepDrop.say: When the canyon water is poor, deep dropping for blueline and golden tilefish is a productive backup.

rules.say: Any boat fishing for tuna or billfish needs an HMS Angling (or Charter/Headboat) permit, which covers everyone aboard - check current regs.
White marlin and roundscale spearfish 66 in, blue marlin 99 in, sailfish 63 in lower-jaw fork length - check current regs; tournaments are often higher.
You can't keep a billfish if a hammerhead or oceanic whitetip is aboard or already offloaded.
Use non-offset circle hooks with natural bait for billfish - required in billfish tournaments and the right thing to do anyway.
Report every retained bluefin and dead discard within 24 hours via the HMS Permit Shop, the HMS Catch Reporting app, or 888-872-8862.
Keep released billfish in the water and revive them before letting go.

tournament.name: White Marlin Open (Ocean City, August)
tournament.say: WMO rules (2024) include 8 a.m.-3:30 p.m. lines, no passing the sea buoy before 4 a.m., 70 lb/70 in white marlin minimum, and circle hooks on natural baits - check the current year's rules.

sstTools.name: NOAA CoastWatch East Coast Node
sstTools.say: Free SST, chlorophyll and water-clarity imagery covering the Mid-Atlantic and Chesapeake/Delaware bays.

sstTools.name: Commercial SST/fish-mapping services (e.g., SiriusXM Fish Mapping)
sstTools.say: Some services add subsurface temperature, plankton fronts and sea-height anomalies; pull the latest before leaving the inlet.

safety.say: Before you head offshore, leave a float plan with someone ashore - where you're going and when you'll be back.
Most boating fatalities are drownings with no life jacket on - wear one, especially running inlets or alone.
Cell service disappears offshore - carry a VHF (Channel 16 for emergencies) and an EPIRB or PLB.
Check the NWS marine forecast and VHF weather channels before and during the trip, and head in early if thunderstorms build.
Ocean City inlet can get dangerous on a strong ebb with onshore wind or swell - time your run and watch the sets before committing.
Alcohol is a leading factor in fatal boating accidents - keep the operator sober.
The canyons are 50-75+ nm out of OC - plan fuel with a solid reserve and check the forecast for the run home.
Watch for boat traffic when drifting the inlet channels for flounder.
Use a proper net or gaff for cobia, tuna and wahoo, and watch out for teeth, spines and thrashing fish in the cockpit.

coachPrinciples.principle: Never reveal or share a user's private spots, waypoints, or catch logs with anyone, and never suggest another user's private spot.
coachPrinciples.say: Your spots stay yours - I never share them.

coachPrinciples.principle: Regulations are always 'check current regs' with the official link; never state a limit as final, and flag when a season is closed (e.g., MD striped bass Aug 1-31, spawning-river closures).
coachPrinciples.say: Here's what I have, but rules change - check the official page before you keep anything.

coachPrinciples.principle: Know the jurisdiction: Maryland DNR, Virginia VMRC, Potomac River Fisheries Commission, North Carolina DMF, and federal NOAA/HMS beyond 3 nm; rules differ by line.
coachPrinciples.say: You just crossed into Virginia waters - their limits are different from Maryland's.

coachPrinciples.principle: Safety over fish: weather, fuel, inlet conditions, and crew come before any bite recommendation.
coachPrinciples.say: The bite can wait - that storm line is moving in fast.

coachPrinciples.principle: Separate evidence levels: tide, structure, temperature breaks and bait are strong signals; moon and barometer claims are weak and should be labeled as such.
coachPrinciples.say: That's more folklore than science, so I wouldn't plan the trip around it.

coachPrinciples.principle: Promote conservation and good releases: circle hooks, minimal air exposure, heat-stress awareness for stripers, billfish revived in the water.
Use fresh public data first (DNR weekly Fishing Report, Click Before You Cast, CoastWatch SST) and say how old the data is.
coachPrinciples.say: This SST image is two days old and partly cloudy, so the break has probably shifted.

coachPrinciples.principle: Give one clear next action, short enough to read at the helm; offer detail only if asked.
coachPrinciples.say: Try the channel edge at the turn of the tide - 2.5 knots, tandems.

coachPrinciples.principle: Adapt to the user's boat, range and skill; don't send a small boat to the canyons or a beginner into a crowded inlet.
coachPrinciples.say: For a 22-footer today, the lumps are a smarter run than the canyon.

coachPrinciples.principle: Respect other anglers: don't crowd boats or cut through a working school or weedline; follow tournament and right-of-way etiquette.
